Snowflake Display Shelf

Build a snowflake-shaped display shelf for miniature houses and seasonal decor. This 36-inch design uses 1x4 boards, an open back, and a single cut diagram with measurements rounded to the nearest 1/8 inch.

Jump to:TopPlanBrags

Why we love this plan

Snowflake Display Shelf

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:18
Instaread

A snowflake shelf turns favorite little houses, bottle-brush trees, and other lightweight decorations into a winter display. This design stands 1x4 boards on edge to create 3-1/2-inch-deep shelves.

The 36-inch layout has a continuous horizontal spine, four angled spokes, and outward-facing middle points built from longer and shorter pieces. Use wood glue and 1-1/4-inch brad nails to attach the joints. Where direct access is unavailable, angle brads across the joint from the front and back faces into the adjoining board.

Design draft: The beauty image is an AI-generated styling visualization. Dry-fit the rounded cuts before batch cutting. Wall mounting and load capacity still require verification.

Inspired by reader builds

These shelves were inspired by the snowflake displays shared in DIY Christmas Projects (Fireman Joe) and Christmas Items to Sell (Mikes Planters). Their photos show the shelf construction that guided this separate plan. Also see Snowflake shelf, where the builder made ten shelves for family Christmas gifts.

The new drawing uses a 36-inch width and 1x4 boards. It is a new dimensional interpretation; the reader submissions do not supply the cut lengths or hidden fastening details.

Display and finish

Choose a painted or natural-wood finish to suit your holiday decor. Sand before assembly, test the finish on an offcut, and let it cure according to the manufacturer. The horizontal sections provide display ledges; sloping boards are not level shelves.

Cut reference diagram

Use the labeled profiles below with the cut list. B1 and B2 are measured long point to short point along the same straight edge, with parallel end cuts. Dry-fit the rounded lengths before batch cutting.

Shopping List

3 - 1x4 boards, 8 feet long (actual 3/4 inch x 3-1/2 inches)
Wood glue
1-1/4 inch brad nails
Sandpaper and your choice of primer/paint or wood finish
Wall-hanging hardware suitable for the wall and finished shelf

Cut List

All pieces are 1x4 boards (actual 3/4 inch x 3-1/2 inches). Lengths below are rounded reference dimensions to the nearest 1/8 inch; dry-fit and trim to close the joints. Angles are OFF SQUARE. See preparation instructions for board orientation.

A1 — 1 at 36 inches. Both ends square; continuous horizontal spine.

A2 — 4 at approximately 17-3/8 inches along each FINISHED STRAIGHT SIDE EDGE. Outer end square. Center end: 30-degree main cut plus 60-degree toe trim, creating a 3/8-inch-high center mating face. Measure along the straight edge from the square end to its intersection with the center cut. Make two as shown and two mirrored. Follow the two-cut profile in step 1.

B1 — 6 at 7 inches, LONG POINT TO SHORT POINT along the SAME STRAIGHT EDGE. Both ends 30 degrees, cuts PARALLEL. Either straight side edge measures 7 inches.

B2 — 6 at approximately 6-1/8 inches, LONG POINT TO SHORT POINT along the SAME STRAIGHT EDGE. Both ends 30 degrees, cuts PARALLEL. Mirror the B1 cut direction for the paired point.

C — 12 at approximately 3-3/4 inches along the LONGER STRAIGHT EDGE, from the square outer end to the long point of the 30-degree inner cut. Other end square. Make six as shown and six mirrored.

Step-by-step instructions

Build the Snowflake Display Shelf

Step 1

Lay out the continuous spine and four angled spokes

Cut and dry-fit sample joints before batch cutting. A1 runs continuously through the center at 36 inches. Fit two A2 spokes above it and two below it, maintaining 60-degree spacing. Their rounded side-edge length is 17-3/8 inches. The main center cut bears against A1; the small 60-degree toe trim lets each upper or lower pair meet on the centerline. Keep all front edges flush. Dimensions are rounded to 1/8 inch; trim to fit the actual board thickness.

Save
Step 2

Fit the outward-facing middle points

Lay out the middle joints at nominal 7-inch centerline locations on the arms. Each point uses one B1 long piece at 7 inches and one B2 short piece at approximately 6-1/8 inches. B1 continues to form the point, and B2 meets its side. Repeat around the shelf with all six points facing outward. Dry-fit and trim the rounded cuts as needed. Measure both pieces long point to short point along the same straight edge; both 30-degree end cuts are parallel. Attach with wood glue and 1-1/4 inch brad nails.

Save
Step 3

Add the outer fork branches

Add the twelve C branches in mirrored pairs. Their centerlines intersect the arms at 14 inches from the center. Each branch has one 30-degree end and one square outer end, with a rounded long-edge length of 3-3/4 inches. Keep all front edges flush and dry-fit before fastening.

Save
Step 4

Glue and nail the joints, then finish

After dry-fitting, apply wood glue to each mating surface and attach with 1-1/4 inch brad nails. Where no direct attachment point is accessible, angle brads across the joint from both the front and back faces into the adjoining board. Position each brad so its tip stays inside the wood. Keep all front edges flush and clamp the assembly flat while the glue cures. Fill nail holes, sand, and apply your finish. Select wall-hanging hardware suitable for the finished shelf and wall construction; no tested load rating has been established.

Finishing steps

How to Finish Your Project

A great finish can transform a project and turn it into something marvelous. This is perhaps the most important stage!

Interior

Paint Finish

⌄
  1. Fill all exposed holes with wood filler. Slightly overfill each hole and let the filler dry completely.
  2. Sand the entire project in the direction of the wood grain with medium-grit sandpaper. Remove the sanding residue.
  3. Inspect the project, add more wood filler where needed, let it dry, then sand again.
  4. Remove all residue with a vacuum fitted with a soft-bristled brush, followed by a damp, lint-free cloth. Let the wood dry.
  5. Use either paint with primer included or apply a separate primer first. Apply the first coat with a quality synthetic-bristle brush or foam roller and let it dry completely.
  6. Lightly sand with fine-grit sandpaper and remove all sanding residue before applying the next coat.
  7. Add paint coats until the color and sheen are consistent. For high-use projects, choose a durable trim or door paint.
Interior

Stain Finish

⌄
  1. Do not fill the exposed holes yet. Wood filler can absorb stain differently from the surrounding wood.
  2. Sand the entire project in the direction of the wood grain with medium-grit sandpaper.
  3. Remove all sanding residue with a vacuum fitted with a soft-bristled brush, followed by a damp, lint-free cloth. Let the wood dry.
  4. Apply interior wood stain in the direction of the grain with a foam applicator.
  5. Wipe away excess stain with a clean shop towel or paper cloth. Add stain layers until the desired color is achieved, allowing the required drying time between applications.
  6. After staining, fill exposed holes with a color-matched wood filler if desired.
  7. Protect the finished project with a clear polyurethane top coat.
Exterior

Solid Color or Stain Finish

⌄
  1. Choose an exterior product made for fences or decks and suitable for the project’s exposure.
  2. For a paint-like finish, use an opaque or solid-color product.
  3. For a stained-wood look, use a semi-transparent exterior stain.
  4. Prepare the wood and apply the product exactly as directed on the can, including the recommended number of coats, drying time, and curing time.

Important: Always follow the preparation, application, drying, and safety instructions provided by the product manufacturer.

Ask Ana

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers to common woodworking and project-plan questions.

What wood should I use?＋
Most Ana White plans use common pine, whitewood, or fir because it is affordable, widely available, and beginner friendly. Choose the straightest, driest boards you can find. For outdoor projects, use lumber and a finish suitable for your climate.
What tools do I really need?＋
Many projects can be built with a drill, circular saw, tape measure, speed square, clamps, sander, and appropriate safety gear. A miter saw and nailer can make repeated projects faster, but they are not required to begin.
How do I make cleaner, more accurate cuts?＋
Use a sharp blade, support and clamp the board, mark the waste side, and account for the blade kerf. Cut slowly and practice on scrap before cutting your project pieces.
Can I change the dimensions of a plan?＋
Often, yes. Review every shopping-list, cut-list, and assembly dimension before building because changing one measurement may affect several parts. Keep structural supports and safe spans in mind.
